mcqs.question: A Bold toolbar button calls `document.applyBold()` directly. What breaks first when you also need a keyboard shortcut, a menu item, and undo support for the same action?
options: Each new trigger has to duplicate knowledge of exactly which method to call and with what arguments, and none of them has anywhere to record how to reverse the action
Nothing breaks — direct calls scale fine to any number of triggers and requirements
document.applyBold() must be rewritten as a static method before any of this is possible
Keyboard shortcuts cannot call the same underlying method as a button click in any language
mcqs.explanation: Every new trigger duplicates the same coupling to the receiver and its exact call signature, and none of them has a natural place to also remember how to undo the action. Nothing here requires a static method, and keyboard shortcuts calling the same method as a button is entirely normal in every mainstream language.

mcqs.question: In a two-stack undo/redo implementation, why does performing a brand-new action after an undo typically clear the redo stack?
options: It's an arbitrary UI convention with no structural reason behind it
The redo stack has a hardcoded maximum size that the new action always exceeds
The command sequence has branched, so the old redo history no longer matches the current document state
Redo stacks are cleared automatically every few seconds regardless of user action
mcqs.explanation: Once a new action executes after an undo, the document has diverged from the path the redo stack assumed — replaying the old redo commands would no longer produce a consistent result, so clearing it is a structural necessity, not an arbitrary rule, a size limit, or a timer.

mcqs.question: You need to let a user reverse a specific past action in a text editor. Which pattern is the better fit, and why?
options: Strategy, because undo is just another interchangeable algorithm
Either works equally well since both hold an object behind an interface
Command — it encapsulates the action, its receiver, and its arguments as an object that can be stored and reversed later
Neither pattern applies to undo functionality
mcqs.explanation: Command is built for exactly this: representing a specific past action as a stored object, complete with what it acted on, so it can be reversed later via undo(). Strategy is about swapping which computation runs right now, not remembering and reversing a specific past request — the two aren't interchangeable here despite similar shapes.

mcqs.question: A `BoldCommand` stores a text range as raw character positions `[10, 20]`. After another command inserts text earlier in the document, the user undoes the bold command. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing — undo() always operates on the exact same characters regardless of intervening edits
The undo() call will throw a runtime error whenever the document has changed
The CommandHistory stack automatically re-validates and fixes stale ranges before calling undo()
undo() removes bold from whatever text now sits at positions 10-20, which may no longer be the text that was originally bolded
mcqs.explanation: Raw index-based ranges drift when earlier edits shift content, so undo() faithfully but incorrectly acts on whatever is now at those positions. There's no automatic re-validation or guaranteed error — the fix is anchors that move with edits, or snapshotting exactly what changed instead of a position.
